extraction.name: SciQ
extraction.description: A dataset of 13,679 multiple choice science exam questions crowdsourced using a novel method that leverages domain-specific text and existing questions to generate high-quality, domain-targeted questions with plausible answer distractors.
extraction.creator: Johannes Welbl, Nelson F. Liu, Matt Gardner
extraction.rai:dataCollection: A two-step crowdsourcing process was used: (1) crowd workers were shown filtered passages from science textbooks and asked to formulate questions about them, with three passage options provided per worker; (2) another worker took the generated question-answer pair and produced three distractor answers, aided by a model trained to predict good distractors. The process leveraged a corpus of 28 science study textbooks from online learning resources including CK-12 and OpenStax, covering biology, chemistry, earth science and physics from elementary to college introductory level.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Science study textbooks from online learning resources. The corpus consisted of 28 books from CK-12 and OpenStax shared under Creative Commons License, covering biology, chemistry, earth science and physics, spanning elementary level to college introductory material. Paragraphs were filtered using a rule-based document filter before being shown to crowd workers.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Two-step crowdsourcing process: (1) Workers shown three filtered textbook paragraphs, select one and formulate a question with answer (6-30 words question, up to 3 words answer, no yes/no questions, querying general principles). (2) Second worker takes question/answer and produces three distractors aided by ML model predictions. Guidelines specified desirable characteristics with examples of good/bad questions. Workers could reject irrelevant documents and provide feedback via contact email.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Human evaluation showing humans cannot distinguish crowdsourced questions from original questions. Quality validated through comparison with real science exams.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: Two workers per item: one for question/answer generation, one for distractor generation
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: Rule-based document filter for passage selection (15 filtering rules including lexical, grammatical, pragmatical and complexity-based rules). Feature-based random forest ranking model trained on real science exam questions to predict and suggest answer distractors.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The dataset shows limitations in neural model performance compared to simple information retrieval baselines. TableILP performance is substantially worse on SciQ because it uses a hand-collected set of background knowledge that does not cover the topics in SciQ.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is useful for training, validation, and testing in science QA tasks. It can be used to investigate neural model performance in medium-sized data settings and to augment training data for answering real science exam questions. The dataset was randomly shuffled and split into training, validation and test portions.
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The dataset is released for future research with possible future work including systematic exploration of multitask settings and further bootstrapping.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The dataset construction involved a two-step crowdsourcing process: (1) workers selected from candidate passages filtered from science textbooks and generated questions with answers, and (2) other workers produced three distractor answers aided by a model trained to predict good answer distractors. The method leveraged model suggestions for document selection and answer distractor choice to aid the human question generation process.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: A rule-based document filter was applied to science textbook paragraphs to identify suitable text for question generation. The filter classified individual sentences and accepted paragraphs if a minimum number of sentences passed. Filter rules included lexical, grammatical, pragmatical and complexity-based criteria, such as filtering out questions, sentences without verb phrases, those with modal verbs, imperative phrases, demonstrative pronouns, personal pronouns other than third-person, sentences with specific length constraints, and those containing instructional vocabulary.
